name: Blosc (c-blosc)
baseline: memcpy (single ctypes.memmove call; Blosc's own named baseline)
workload: python-blosc bench/compress_ptr.py: NumPy arrays of 10**8 int64/float64 elements (about 800 MB; arange, linspace and random distributions), clevel 5, 24 threads, compress and decompress through Blosc 1.11.2 (the C library) with each codec and the shuffle/bitshuffle filters, timed against a plain ctypes.memmove() copy of the array.
claimed_speedup: memcpy via ctypes.memmove 0.276 s (2.70 GB/s). arange data: blosclz+shuffle 17.77 GB/s compress and 27.18 GB/s decompress (ratio 57.1x); lz4+shuffle 22.58 / 22.03 GB/s (68.6x); zstd+shuffle 7.97 / 32.71 GB/s (156.7x). random data: lz4+shuffle 11.02 / 26.03 GB/s (4.5x); blosclz+shuffle 8.21 / 44.29 GB/s (3.9x). Roughly 6.6x memcpy compress and 10x memcpy decompress for blosclz+shuffle on arange (derived from page data). Without the shuffle filter blosclz is slower than memcpy: 1.95 / 2.48 GB/s at ratio 1.0x.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2695 v3 @ 2.30GHz (56 cores detected), 24 threads used, CentOS 7.2, Linux 3.10.0 (as printed in the README run)
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; official Python wrapper (python-blosc) and HDF5 filter (hdf5-blosc)
tradeoffs: Meta-compressor: the speedup comes from blocking, the shuffle/bitshuffle filters, SIMD and its own thread pool, and it pays off for typed binary data such as numeric arrays (needs the type size); bundles LZ4, Snappy, Zlib and Zstd. The repository says it is in pure maintenance mode and points to C-Blosc2 for new features. C89 code base.
caveats: The numbers are the project's own, printed in the README of the Python wrapper (python-blosc 1.5.1.dev0 driving Blosc 1.11.2, a 2017 run), with partial methodology: CPU and thread count are stated, the compiler flags of the C library are not (the header only shows Python 3.5.2 built with GCC 4.4.7). The memcpy baseline is one single-threaded ctypes.memmove call while Blosc ran 24 threads, so the ratio mixes parallelism with compression; the arange and linspace arrays are synthetic and extremely compressible (ratio up to 260x with bitshuffle). Without shuffle blosclz is slower than memcpy. The c-blosc2 repo's own bench/results-corex run (2020 beta, no CPU named, 4 MB synthetic data with 19 significant bits) shows the same shape: at 1 thread and clevel 1, decompress 10667.6 MB/s vs memcpy(read) 8289.1 MB/s and compress 4714.6 vs memcpy(write) 4628.8 MB/s. The blosc.org benchmark pages and the 2010 CISE paper are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so they were not read. The Blosc2 successor (github.com/Blosc/c-blosc2) is already in the catalogue at tier C.
found_via: seed-record pass: http://blosc.org/pages/blosc-in-depth (blocked), then the Blosc/c-blosc README and the Benchmarking section of the Blosc/python-blosc README

name: LZ4
workload: lzbench (from @inikep), in-memory, single thread, Silesia corpus: compression and decompression throughput plus compression factor for LZ4 against LZO, QuickLZ, Snappy, Zstandard, LZF and zlib.
claimed_speedup: LZ4 default (v1.9.0): 780 MB/s compress, 4970 MB/s decompress, factor 2.101. zlib deflate 1.2.11 -1: 100 MB/s, 415 MB/s, factor 2.730, so about 7.8x faster compress and 12x faster decompress (derived from page data) at a lower factor. LZ4 HC -9 (v1.9.0): 41 MB/s compress, 4900 MB/s decompress, factor 2.721 vs zlib -6 at 36 MB/s, 445 MB/s, factor 3.099 (about 11x decompress, derived from page data). Also vs Snappy 1.1.4 565 / 1950 MB/s and LZO 2.09 670 / 860 MB/s; memcpy row 13700 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: GCC v8.2.0 on Linux 64-bit (Ubuntu, kernel 4.18.0-17); optimisation flags are not in the README but come from the public lzbench Makefile (-O3)
hardware: Core i7-9700K @ 4.9GHz (with turbo boost), single thread
stars_or_usage: 12.1k stars; README carries a repology packaging-status badge
tradeoffs: Trades ratio for speed: factor 2.101 vs zlib -1 at 2.730 and Zstandard -1 at 2.883 in the same table. LZ4_HC raises the factor with the same decode speed at a large compression cost. Only the last 64 KB of a dictionary is used. The library (lib/) is BSD-2-Clause, the command-line programs are GPL-2.0-or-later.
caveats: The README table is a 2019 run (v1.9.0, GCC 8.2.0) and does not print the build flags; the benchmark program is the public lzbench, whose Makefile builds with -O3. Cross-check from the lzbench 2.4 README (AMD EPYC 9555P, gcc 15.2.0, single thread, lz4 1.10.0): 550 MB/s compress and 3832 MB/s decompress vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 / 297 MB/s (6.2x / 12.9x, derived) and Snappy 1.3.1 at 457 / 976 MB/s (1.2x / 3.9x, derived); the decompression lead holds, the compression lead over Snappy shrinks. Zstandard -1 in the README table compresses slower (515 MB/s) but gives a better factor, so LZ4's win is a speed point, not a dominance over Zstandard. lz4.github.io (the listed URL) is blocked here, so the README on github.com was used.

name: LZHAM (lzham_codec)
workload: lzbench 2.4, in-memory, single thread, silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes): decompression speed and output size of lzham 1.0 -d26 against lzma 26.03 at comparable ratio.
claimed_speedup: lzham 1.0 -d26 -1: 3.16 MB/s compress, 273 MB/s decompress, 54,740,589 bytes (25.83%). lzma 26.03 -4: 13.6 MB/s, 73.7 MB/s, 55,936,064 bytes (26.39%); lzma -2: 23.0 / 70.2 MB/s, 57,082,443 bytes (26.93%). So about 3.7x faster decompression than lzma -4 with 2% smaller output (derived from page data), at about 4.3x slower compression. LZHAM -0: 11.1 / 200 MB/s, 64,089,870 bytes (30.24%). LZMA at -6 and -9 is smaller (49,551,059 and 48,682,482 bytes) and decodes at 78.4 and 78.2 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary), lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; the public lzbench Makefile builds with -O3
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P @ 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
license: Public domain (LICENSE dedication dated 2020-09-15; no SPDX id)
stars_or_usage: 729 stars; shipped as a 7-Zip codec plugin per the README
tradeoffs: Very asymmetric: slow, memory-hungry compressor aimed at offline use (README: about 982 MB for a 64 MB dictionary) and a decoder with a high start-up cost, only faster than LZMA beyond roughly 1-13 KB of compressed input. Decodes slower than zlib (lzbench: 273 MB/s vs zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 318 MB/s). C++03, no strict aliasing required (-fno-strict-aliasing). Public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
caveats: lzbench exposes only LZHAM levels -0 and -1 (not the default uber -m4 or the extreme parser), so the README's 'ratio similar to LZMA with 1.5x-8x faster decompression' is only partly reproduced: LZHAM -1 beats lzma -4 and -2 on size and decode speed, but lzma -6 and -9 are 10-12% smaller than LZHAM -1. The README's own 10GB-benchmark figures (7zip-LZHAM 9.38 32-bit, 64 MB dictionary: LZHAM -mx=9 3,573,782,721 bytes with archive test time 71.292 s vs LZMA -mx=9 3,560,052,414 bytes at 223.050 s, about 3.1x) carry no hardware or compiler and mattmahoney.net is blocked here. The improved branch richgel999/lzham_codec_devel is already in the catalogue at tier C on that README evidence; this record is the stable v1.x repository with the lzbench run. The most recent commit seen (2022-01-03) is 'Update README.md'. The listed code.google.com/p/lzham URL is the old alpha and was not opened.

name: LZMAT
workload: lzbench 1.8, in-memory, one core, silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes), compress and decompress throughput and output size of lzmat 1.01 against zlib, LZO, LZ4 and Snappy.
claimed_speedup: lzmat 1.01: 38 MB/s compress, 479 MB/s decompress, 76,485,353 bytes (36.09%). zlib 1.2.11 -1: 119 MB/s, 383 MB/s, 77,259,029 bytes (36.45%); zlib -6: 35 MB/s, 407 MB/s, 68,228,431 bytes (32.19%). Decompression is about 1.25x faster than zlib -1 and 1.18x faster than zlib -6 (derived from page data) at a size close to -1; compression is about 3.1x slower than zlib -1 and roughly level with -6. It does not beat LZO: lzo1x -999 gives 75,301,903 bytes (35.53%) at 8.76 MB/s compress and 827 MB/s decompress, and lz4 1.9.2 decompresses at 4448 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: clang 9.0.1; lzbench 1.8 with -t16,16 -eall; flags come from the public lzbench Makefile and were not re-checked at that tag
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later copyleft. Slow compressor (38 MB/s). Pointer arithmetic goes through 32-bit MP_U32 types, which lzbench had to patch for 64-bit builds. A single-commit mirror of release 1.01 (2008).
caveats: Tier capped at C although the harness is reproducible: lzbench lists lzmat under 'security issues and/or no longer maintained' and warns that it contains bugs (decompression error, returns 0) and can segfault with GCC 4.9+ -O3, so the numbers do not describe a trustworthy codec. The lead is narrow (decompression only, about 1.2x over zlib) and the codec loses to LZO, LZ4 and Snappy in the same table. lzbench 2.4 no longer prints a lzmat row; this is the last tag that does (v1.8.1; v1.5 and v1.7.3 gave 24 MB/s / 288-294 MB/s on older hardware). The author's own claims on matcode.com returned 403 and the mirror seen in search results (autohotkey.com) is blocked, so no first-party numbers were read; the GitHub repo page carries no benchmarks.

name: libbzip2 (bzip2)
baseline: ppmd8 (7-Zip PPMd var.I, ppmd8 26.03 as built in lzbench), the PPM family the bzip2 manual compares itself with
workload: lzbench 2.4, in-memory, single thread, silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes): compress and decompress speed and output size of bzip2 1.0.8 against ppmd8 26.03 (and lzma 26.03).
claimed_speedup: bzip2 1.0.8 -9: 12.7 MB/s compress, 35.5 MB/s decompress, 54,572,811 bytes (25.75%). ppmd8 26.03 -4: 12.8 / 11.5 MB/s, 51,241,932 bytes (24.18%); ppmd8 -1: 15.7 / 14.0 MB/s, 55,803,295 bytes (26.33%); ppmd8 -9: 2.61 / 2.55 MB/s, 48,207,763 bytes (22.75%). Decompression is about 3.1x faster than ppmd8 -4, 2.5x faster than ppmd8 -1 (with 2% smaller output) and 13.9x faster than ppmd8 -9 (derived from page data); compression is level with ppmd8 -4, 4.9x faster than -9 and 1.2x slower than -1. Against lzma 26.03 -9 (2.55 / 78.2 MB/s, 22.97%) bzip2 -9 compresses about 5x faster but decompresses 2.2x slower and is 12% larger (derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15 release binary), lzbench options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; the public lzbench Makefile builds with -O3
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P @ 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
license: bzip2-1.0.6 (the 'bzip2 and libbzip2 License v1.0.6', BSD-style, as shown on the GitLab page)
stars_or_usage: GitLab fork archived; GitHub mirror libarchive/bzip2 has 64 stars; version 1.0.8 dated 2019-07-13 in lzbench
tradeoffs: Block-sorting (Burrows-Wheeler) compressor with a better ratio than zlib (25.75% at -9 vs 31.92% for zlib 1.3.2 -9 in the same table) but slow decoding (35.5 MB/s vs 318 MB/s for zlib -9) and a single-threaded reference implementation. The patent-free, library-callable (libbz2) incumbent that lbzip2 and bzip3 are measured against.
caveats: The project's own claim is in the bzip2 manual: ratio within 10-15% of the best available techniques (the PPM family) at about twice the compression speed and six times the decompression speed. That text was seen only as a WebSearch snippet repeated on HPC documentation sites, because bzip.org and sourceware.org/bzip2 are blocked here, and the 2x and 6x figures do not appear on the benchmark page. lzbench reproduces the decompression half (2.5x to 14x depending on the ppmd8 level) but not the compression half (level to 1.2x slower at similar size). The comparison is against one PPMd implementation, and PPMd -4 gives a 6% smaller output. bzip2 is slower or larger than modern codecs in the same table (lbzip2 2.6.5 -9 compresses 22.4 MB/s and decompresses 47.0 MB/s at the same size; lzma 26.03 -4 and zstd 1.5.7 -18 reach similar or smaller outputs at 26.39% and 25.14% while decompressing 73.7 and 1175 MB/s, though zstd -18 compresses at only 4.13 MB/s). The GitLab repository is the archived 1.1+ development fork; the 1.0.8 sources live at sourceware.org (blocked), so last_commit is unknown. The record fills the project's slot; its value is as the reference implementation, not as a fast codec.
